\chapter{Son and Daughter, Two Different Roots}
\label{ch:te-son-and-daughter}
\hlchaptermodality{36}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say son and daughter in Telugu, and show that they trace to two different Proto-Dravidian roots rather than one shared root.}

Line up \te{కొడుకు} and \te{కూతురు} against their two separate Proto-Dravidian roots, trace \te{కొడుకు}'s own root sideways to \te{కోడలు} (\textquotedblleft{}daughter-in-law\textquotedblright{}), and trace \te{కూతురు}'s root across the family to Kannada's word for infant.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[koḍuku]{\te{కొడుకు} (koḍuku) — \textquotedblleft{}son,\textquotedblright{} and the unexpected word it shares a root with}

\label{lesson:TE-C36-koduku}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Kuṭumbaṁ}, family; \emph{snēhituḍu}, friend. Now the two words for your own children — and Telugu does not build them the tidy way you might expect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కొడుకు}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{కొడుకు}} — \emph{koḍuku} — \textbf{son}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{వాడి} \te{కొడుకు} \te{వయసెంత}?} — \emph{vāḍi koḍuku vayasenta?} — \textquotedblleft{}How old is his son?\textquotedblright{} — the verbless age question you already know, asked about someone else's child.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{కొడుకు}} is inherited from Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*kōẓ-}, \textquotedblleft{}young, tender.\textquotedblright{} You might expect \textquotedblleft{}daughter,\textquotedblright{} Telugu's other child-word, to share that same root with a different ending — that is exactly the shape Kannada's \emph{magu/maga/ magalu} takes. Telugu does not do that. The very same \textbf{*kōẓ-} root instead gives Telugu \textbf{\te{కోడలు}} (\emph{kōḍalu}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{daughter-in-law}\textquotedblright{} — the woman a son marries, not the daughter a parent has. So \emph{koḍuku} and \emph{kōḍalu} are true cognates, one root apart; \emph{koḍuku} and \emph{kūturu} — son and daughter — are not related to each other at all. The next lesson takes up \emph{kūturu}'s own, separate root.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}koḍuku\textquotedblright{} — son
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vāḍi koḍuku vayasenta?\textquotedblright{} — how old is his son?
  \item the unexpected cognate — \textquotedblleft{}koḍuku … kōḍalu\textquotedblright{} — son, daughter-in-law
  \item three words for people — \textquotedblleft{}kuṭumbaṁ … snēhituḍu … koḍuku\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}son.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Koḍuku}.) What Proto-Dravidian root does it come from, and what other Telugu word shares that exact root? (\textbf{*kōẓ-}, \textquotedblleft{}young, tender\textquotedblright{} — shared with \textbf{\te{కోడలు}}, \textquotedblleft{}daughter-in-law,\textquotedblright{} not with \textquotedblleft{}daughter\textquotedblright{} itself.) Ask \textquotedblleft{}how old is his son?\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Vāḍi koḍuku vayasenta?})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kūturu]{\te{కూతురు} (kūturu) — \textquotedblleft{}daughter,\textquotedblright{} on a root all its own}

\label{lesson:TE-C36-kuuturu}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Koḍuku}'s root turned up again inside a completely different Telugu word. This word's root does something even less expected: it turns up inside a different \textbf{language}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కూతురు}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{కూతురు}} — \emph{kūturu} — \textbf{daughter}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నా} \te{కూతురు}.} — \emph{nā kūturu.} — \textquotedblleft{}My daughter.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{కూతురు}} is inherited from Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*kūnttu} — a root with \textbf{no connection} to \emph{koḍuku}'s \textbf{*kōẓ-}. Telugu's two child-words are not a matched pair; they are two separate inheritances that happen to sit side by side in the same sentence.

\emph{Kūturu}'s cousin is not in Telugu at all. Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಕೂಸು}} (\emph{kūsu}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{infant, maiden},\textquotedblright{} answers to the very same root. So the word a Telugu speaker uses for \textquotedblleft{}my daughter\textquotedblright{} and the word a Kannada speaker uses for \textquotedblleft{}the baby\textquotedblright{} are, underneath, one and the same — a reminder that a cognate does not have to keep the same \emph{sense} as it crosses a language boundary, only the same root.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nā kūturu\textquotedblright{} — my daughter
  \item son, then daughter — \textquotedblleft{}koḍuku … kūturu\textquotedblright{} — two unrelated roots
  \item the cross-language cousin — \textquotedblleft{}kūturu … kūsu\textquotedblright{} — daughter, infant
  \item friend, son, daughter — \textquotedblleft{}snēhituḍu … koḍuku … kūturu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my daughter.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nā kūturu}.) Does \emph{kūturu} share a root with \emph{koḍuku}? (\textbf{No} — two separate Proto-Dravidian roots.) What word in another Dravidian language answers to \emph{kūturu}'s own root, and what does it mean there? (\textbf{Kannada \te{కూసు}} \emph{kūsu}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{infant, maiden}.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
